# Exercise 2.5 — Scaling, transformation and features {#sec-scaling}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In R or in Python
Pick a tab and stay in it. The two tabs are the same exercise — the same
sections, the same tasks, the same numbers — so complete either one.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- put features measured on different scales onto a comparable one, three
  different ways, and say what each one assumes;
- predict which scaler an extreme value will damage, and check your prediction;
- treat the log and the square root as one family rather than two tricks;
- say what a squared term buys a linear model and why the model is still
  linear;
- count the columns a feature-engineering step adds, and say why the count
  matters.

## Why this, here

@sec-imputation left a complete table. Its three numeric columns are still
measured in unrelated units: `age` in years, `BMI` in kg/m², `systolic_BP` in
mmHg. Nothing is wrong with that — but several models behave as though the
numbers were comparable, and will quietly let the column with the widest range
dominate.

Everything in this exercise is still a plain function applied to a whole
column. @sec-pipeline-steps then shows why every single step here is a step
that has to be *fitted*, and what goes wrong when you fit it at the wrong
moment.

## Starting point

Picking up from @sec-imputation: the same cleaning, then median imputation so
nothing is missing, then BMI recomputed from the filled inputs.

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

na_codes <- c("unknown", "?", "not recorded", "N/A", "-999")
num_cols <- c("age", "height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP")

gp <- read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if_else(as.character(.x) %in% na_codes,
                                        NA_character_, as.character(.x)))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols), as.numeric)) |>
  mutate(
    height_cm = if_else(height_cm < 3, height_cm * 100, height_cm),
    age       = if_else(age > 120, NA_real_, age),
    weight_kg = if_else(weight_kg > 300, NA_real_, weight_kg)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(num_cols),
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x))) |>
  mutate(BMI = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2)

scale_cols <- c("age", "BMI", "systolic_BP")
sapply(gp[scale_cols], range) |> round(1)
```

Three columns, three ranges, none of them comparable: `age` runs 19 to 91,
`BMI` 15.8 to 44.4, `systolic_BP` 104 to 165. `systolic_BP` spans the widest
numeric distance, and to a model that measures distances — anything using a
Euclidean distance, and anything regularised — that width is indistinguishable
from importance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Three scalers

#### Min-Max: squeeze into [0, 1]

Subtract the minimum, divide by the range. Every value lands between 0 and 1,
and the shape of the distribution is untouched.

```{r}
minmax <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
}

X_mm <- gp |> mutate(across(all_of(scale_cols), minmax))

sapply(X_mm[scale_cols], range)
```

#### Standard: centre and divide by the standard deviation

Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. Each column now has mean
0 and standard deviation 1. Values are not bounded — an extreme observation
stays extreme, which is usually what you want.

```{r}
X_ss <- gp |>
  mutate(across(all_of(scale_cols), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))

round(rbind(
  mean = sapply(X_ss[scale_cols], mean),
  sd   = sapply(X_ss[scale_cols], sd)
), 3)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## One honest difference between the two tabs
R's `scale()` divides by the **sample** standard deviation, with $n-1$ in the
denominator; `scikit-learn`'s `StandardScaler` divides by the **population**
standard deviation, with $n$. On 180 rows that is a difference of about 0.3%,
which is why the standardised outlier below reads 3.03 in R and 3.04 in Python.
Neither is wrong. It is worth knowing that a "standardised" column is not one
single defined thing.
:::

#### Robust: use the median and the IQR

Subtract the median, divide by the interquartile range. Both are quantities an
extreme value barely moves, which is the whole idea.

```{r}
robust <- function(x) {
  (x - median(x)) / IQR(x)
}

X_rs <- gp |> mutate(across(all_of(scale_cols), robust))

round(rbind(
  median = sapply(X_rs[scale_cols], median),
  max    = sapply(X_rs[scale_cols], max)
), 2)
```

### What the one bad value does to each

`BMI` has a genuine high extreme — the heaviest patient in the cohort, not a
typo. @sec-cleaning already removed the errors; what is left is real. Watch
what each scaler does with a value you must **not** throw away.

```{r}
i <- which.max(gp$BMI)

data.frame(
  scaler  = c("Min-Max", "Standard", "Robust"),
  outlier = c(X_mm$BMI[i], X_ss$BMI[i], X_rs$BMI[i]),
  median_row = c(median(X_mm$BMI), median(X_ss$BMI), median(X_rs$BMI)),
  bulk_max_excl_outlier = c(max(X_mm$BMI[-i]), max(X_ss$BMI[-i]),
                            max(X_rs$BMI[-i]))
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

Read the last column against the second, and be precise about what you see.

Under **Min-Max** the extreme is pinned at 1 by definition, and because it sets
the maximum, every other value is divided by a range it stretched. The rest of
the cohort now spans 0 to about 0.88, so a single patient has claimed roughly
an eighth of the available scale. Under **Standard** and **Robust** nothing is
pinned: the extreme sits out at about 3.0 standard deviations and 2.4
interquartile ranges respectively, which is an honest description of a value
that far from the centre rather than an arbitrary ceiling.

So the three are not as different here as the usual advice implies, because
this extreme is only moderately extreme — it is the heaviest patient, not a
typo. The difference appears when it gets worse. Suppose one weight had been
recorded with a digit in front of it and had slipped past @sec-cleaning:

```{r}
worse <- gp$BMI
worse[i] <- gp$BMI[i] * 3

rbind(
  `bulk max, Min-Max`  = c(now   = max(minmax(gp$BMI)[-i]),
                           worse = max(minmax(worse)[-i])),
  `bulk max, Standard` = c(max(as.numeric(scale(gp$BMI))[-i]),
                           max(as.numeric(scale(worse))[-i])),
  `bulk max, Robust`   = c(max(robust(gp$BMI)[-i]),
                           max(robust(worse)[-i]))
) |> round(2)
```

**Min-Max** collapses: the bulk maximum falls from 0.88 to 0.21, because the
range it divides by is now set entirely by the bad row, so the real data is
squeezed towards zero. **Standard** shrinks too, from 2.40 to about 1.34, since
the standard deviation is inflated by the squared distance of that one point.
**Robust** does not move at all — 1.91 before and 1.91 after — because the
median and the interquartile range cannot be shifted by a single extreme value,
which is the entire reason it exists.

That is the rule worth keeping: Min-Max is the most fragile, Standard is
affected but less so, and Robust is indifferent.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The choice is about the column, not the algorithm
Robust scaling is not uniformly better. If a column has no extreme values,
Min-Max and Standard give you a bounded or a familiar scale and nothing is
lost. Reach for Robust when you have looked at the distribution and seen a tail
— which is why @sec-histograms came first.
:::

### Task 1 — Scale, and measure the damage

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
i <- which.max(gp$BMI)

for (nm in c("minmax", "standard", "robust")) {
  z <- switch(nm,
    minmax   = minmax(gp$BMI),
    standard = as.numeric(scale(gp$BMI)),
    robust   = ______(gp$BMI)
  )
  cat(nm, "outlier", round(z[i], 2),
      " bulk max", round(max(z[______]), 2), "\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the helper defined earlier in this chapter. The second
excludes one position from a vector — a minus sign does it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
i <- which.max(gp$BMI)

for (nm in c("minmax", "standard", "robust")) {
  z <- switch(nm,
    minmax   = minmax(gp$BMI),
    standard = as.numeric(scale(gp$BMI)),
    robust   = robust(gp$BMI)
  )
  cat(nm, "outlier", round(z[i], 2),
      " bulk max", round(max(z[-i]), 2), "\n")
}
```

The gap between the outlier and the bulk maximum is the diagnostic: 1.00
against 0.88 under Min-Max, 3.03 against 2.40 under Standard, 2.41 against 1.91
under Robust.
:::
:::

### Transformation: changing the shape, not the scale

Scaling moves a distribution and stretches it. It does not change its shape: a
skewed column scaled three ways is still skewed three ways. Changing the shape
takes a non-linear function.

Base R has no `skewness()`, so define it once — the third moment over the
standard deviation cubed:

```{r}
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^1.5
}

cat("BMI skew, as recorded:", round(skewness(gp$BMI), 2), "\n")
cat("after square root    :", round(skewness(sqrt(gp$BMI)), 2), "\n")
cat("after log            :", round(skewness(log(gp$BMI)), 2), "\n")
```

0.47 as recorded, 0.21 after the square root, −0.04 after the log. Scaling, for
contrast, leaves skewness **exactly** where it was — subtracting a constant and
dividing by a constant cannot change a shape:

```{r}
cat("min-max scaled :", round(skewness(minmax(gp$BMI)), 2), "\n")
cat("standardised   :", round(skewness(as.numeric(scale(gp$BMI))), 2), "\n")
```

Both still 0.47.

#### Log and square root are the same idea at different strengths

It is tempting to learn these as separate recipes. They are one family. Raising
a column to a power $\lambda$ covers all of them: $\lambda = 1$ leaves the data
alone, $\lambda = 0.5$ is the square root, $\lambda = 0$ is the log, and
$\lambda = 2$ squares it. Smaller $\lambda$ pulls a long right tail in harder.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
powers <- c("square (2)" = 2, "none (1)" = 1, "sqrt (0.5)" = 0.5, "log (0)" = 0)

purrr::imap_dfr(powers, function(lam, nm) {
  v <- if (lam == 0) log(gp$BMI) else gp$BMI^lam
  data.frame(label = nm, value = as.numeric(scale(v)))
}) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = names(powers))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Each panel is standardised, so only the shape differs. Read left to right and
you are turning one dial. Choosing between log and square root is choosing how
far to turn it — not choosing between two unrelated techniques.

One constraint comes with the family: the log of zero is undefined and the log
of a negative number does not exist. `BMI` is strictly positive so it is safe
here, but a column containing zeros — a count of previous admissions, say —
needs `log1p`, or a transformation built to tolerate zeros.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Feature engineering: why would $x^2$ work?

A linear model fits

$$\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

which is a straight line in $x$. If the real relationship bends, a straight
line cannot follow it. Add a squared column and you fit

$$\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2$$

which is a curve in $x$ — and still a **linear model**, because "linear" refers
to the parameters, not the features. $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ still enter as
plain multipliers, so the fitting is the same arithmetic it always was. You
changed the data, not the algorithm.

Here is the thing it buys, on a relationship that genuinely bends:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.8
set.seed(7)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(120, -3, 3))
d$y <- 2 + 0.5 * d$x + 1.2 * d$x^2 + rnorm(120, 0, 1.5)

straight <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
curved   <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2), data = d)

cat("straight line, residual SD:", round(sigma(straight), 2), "\n")
cat("with x squared,            ", round(sigma(curved), 2), "\n")

d |>
  mutate(straight = fitted(straight), curved = fitted(curved)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(straight, curved), names_to = "model", values_to = "fit") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = y), alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit, colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", colour = NULL)
```

A residual spread of about 3.4 for the straight line against 1.4 with the
squared term. The straight line is not wrong so much as unable. It has no
parameter capable of representing curvature, so it averages the bend away and
leaves it in the residuals.

(This is the one place where the two tabs cannot print the same numbers: the
data is simulated, and R and Python draw from different random number
generators, so the Python tab's figures are close but not identical. Everything
computed from `clinic_extract.csv` matches exactly.)

#### What it costs

```{r}
form <- ~ (age + BMI + systolic_BP)^2 +
  I(age^2) + I(BMI^2) + I(systolic_BP^2)

wide <- model.matrix(form, data = gp)[, -1, drop = FALSE]

cat("columns:", length(scale_cols), "->", ncol(wide), "\n")
colnames(wide)
```

Three columns became nine: each original, each square, and each pairwise
product. At degree 2 that is manageable. The growth is quadratic in the number
of features, so the same step on 30 columns gives 495, most of them nearly
duplicates of each other — and every one is a column that can be fitted on the
wrong rows.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Task 2 — Add a term and check it earns its place

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
m1 <- lm(systolic_BP ~ age, data = gp)
m2 <- lm(systolic_BP ~ age + I(age^______), data = gp)

cat("residual SD, straight:", round(sigma(m1), 3), "\n")
cat("residual SD, squared :", round(sigma(______), 3), "\n")
cat("p-value on the squared term:",
    round(summary(m2)$coefficients["I(age^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3), "\n")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the power. The second is the model you just fitted. `I()`
is what stops the formula interpreting `^` as an interaction.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
m1 <- lm(systolic_BP ~ age, data = gp)
m2 <- lm(systolic_BP ~ age + I(age^2), data = gp)

cat("residual SD, straight:", round(sigma(m1), 3), "\n")
cat("residual SD, squared :", round(sigma(m2), 3), "\n")
cat("p-value on the squared term:",
    round(summary(m2)$coefficients["I(age^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3), "\n")
```

This is the useful negative result. The residual spread moves from 10.005 to
10.003 — three thousandths of a mmHg — and the p-value on the squared term is
0.297, nowhere near significant, because this data was simulated with a
straight-line relationship between age and blood pressure. Adding $x^2$ does
not create curvature; it only lets you fit curvature that is there. Compare
with the simulated bending example above, where it was.
:::
:::

### Reflection

1. Min-Max compressed the whole `BMI` column because one value set the maximum.
   Which of the three scalers would you choose for a variable where the extreme
   values are real and clinically important, and why?
2. Standardising a column makes its mean 0 and its standard deviation 1. Does
   it make the column normally distributed? Justify your answer using the
   skewness numbers above.
3. The squared term helped on simulated curved data and not on `age`. What does
   that tell you about adding polynomial terms as a routine step?
4. Degree-2 polynomial features took 3 columns to 9. At what point does that
   stop being a feature-engineering step and start being a problem, and what
   would you look at to decide?

### Stretch

#### Stretch 1 — Find the turning power yourself
Write a loop over $\lambda$ from $-1$ to $2$ in steps of $0.25$, compute the
skewness of `BMI` raised to each power (using the log at $\lambda = 0$), and
plot skewness against $\lambda$. Read the value that brings it closest to zero
off your own plot. You have just performed a Box-Cox transformation by hand.

#### Stretch 2 — Scaling where it changes an answer
Fit a k-nearest-neighbours classifier for `diabetes` on the three numeric
columns, once unscaled and once standardised, and compare. Then explain the
difference in terms of what a Euclidean distance does when one column is
measured in hundreds and another in tens.

### What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the features are on comparable scales, that you chose the scaler
having looked at the distribution rather than by habit, that you know what the
one bad `BMI` value does to each option, and that you can add a polynomial term
and test whether it earned its place.

You cannot claim any of these numbers would survive contact with new data. Every
minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, median and IQR above was computed
from all 180 rows — including the rows you are about to hold out and call a
test set. Each one is a quantity *learned from data*, and learning it from the
wrong rows is the subject of @sec-pipeline-steps.

## Python

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

na_codes = ["unknown", "?", "not recorded", "N/A", "-999"]
num_cols = ["age", "height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP"]

gp_py = pd.read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv",
                    keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
gp_py = gp_py.replace(na_codes, np.nan).replace(-999, np.nan)
for c in num_cols:
    gp_py[c] = pd.to_numeric(gp_py[c], errors="coerce")

gp_py.loc[gp_py.height_cm < 3, "height_cm"] *= 100
gp_py.loc[gp_py.age > 120, "age"] = np.nan
gp_py.loc[gp_py.weight_kg > 300, "weight_kg"] = np.nan

gp_py[num_cols] = gp_py[num_cols].fillna(gp_py[num_cols].median())
gp_py["BMI"] = gp_py.weight_kg / (gp_py.height_cm / 100) ** 2

scale_cols = ["age", "BMI", "systolic_BP"]
print(gp_py[scale_cols].agg(["min", "max"]).round(1))
```

Three columns, three ranges, none of them comparable: `age` runs 19 to 91,
`BMI` 15.8 to 44.4, `systolic_BP` 104 to 165. `systolic_BP` spans the widest
numeric distance, and to a model that measures distances — anything using a
Euclidean distance, and anything regularised — that width is indistinguishable
from importance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Three scalers

#### Min-Max: squeeze into [0, 1]

Subtract the minimum, divide by the range. Every value lands between 0 and 1,
and the shape of the distribution is untouched.

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import (MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler,
                                   RobustScaler)

mm = MinMaxScaler()
X_mm = mm.fit_transform(gp_py[scale_cols])

print(pd.DataFrame(X_mm, columns=scale_cols).agg(["min", "max"]))
```

#### Standard: centre and divide by the standard deviation

Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. Each column now has mean
0 and standard deviation 1. Values are not bounded — an extreme observation
stays extreme, which is usually what you want.

```{python}
ss = StandardScaler()
X_ss = ss.fit_transform(gp_py[scale_cols])

print(pd.DataFrame(X_ss, columns=scale_cols)
        .agg(["mean", "std"]).round(3))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## One honest difference between the two tabs
R's `scale()` divides by the **sample** standard deviation, with $n-1$ in the
denominator; `scikit-learn`'s `StandardScaler` divides by the **population**
standard deviation, with $n$. On 180 rows that is a difference of about 0.3%,
which is why the standardised outlier below reads 3.03 in R and 3.04 in Python.
Neither is wrong. It is worth knowing that a "standardised" column is not one
single defined thing.
:::

#### Robust: use the median and the IQR

Subtract the median, divide by the interquartile range. Both are quantities an
extreme value barely moves, which is the whole idea.

```{python}
rs = RobustScaler()
X_rs = rs.fit_transform(gp_py[scale_cols])

print(pd.DataFrame(X_rs, columns=scale_cols)
        .describe().loc[["50%", "max"]].round(2))
```

### What the one bad value does to each

`BMI` has a genuine high extreme — the heaviest patient in the cohort, not a
typo. @sec-cleaning already removed the errors; what is left is real. Watch
what each scaler does with a value you must **not** throw away.

```{python}
i = int(gp_py["BMI"].argmax())

rows = []
for name, z in [("Min-Max", X_mm[:, 1]), ("Standard", X_ss[:, 1]),
                ("Robust", X_rs[:, 1])]:
    rows.append({"scaler": name,
                 "outlier": z[i],
                 "median_row": np.median(z),
                 "bulk_max_excl_outlier": np.delete(z, i).max()})

print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2).to_string(index=False))
```

Read the last column against the second, and be precise about what you see.

Under **Min-Max** the extreme is pinned at 1 by definition, and because it sets
the maximum, every other value is divided by a range it stretched. The rest of
the cohort now spans 0 to about 0.88, so a single patient has claimed roughly
an eighth of the available scale. Under **Standard** and **Robust** nothing is
pinned: the extreme sits out at about 3.0 standard deviations and 2.4
interquartile ranges respectively, which is an honest description of a value
that far from the centre rather than an arbitrary ceiling.

So the three are not as different here as the usual advice implies, because
this extreme is only moderately extreme — it is the heaviest patient, not a
typo. The difference appears when it gets worse. Suppose one weight had been
recorded with a digit in front of it and had slipped past @sec-cleaning:

```{python}
worse = gp_py["BMI"].to_numpy().copy()
worse[i] = gp_py["BMI"][i] * 3

out = {}
for name, scaler in [("Min-Max", MinMaxScaler()), ("Standard", StandardScaler()),
                     ("Robust", RobustScaler())]:
    now_z   = scaler.fit_transform(gp_py[["BMI"]]).ravel()
    worse_z = scaler.fit_transform(worse.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
    out["bulk max, " + name] = {"now":   np.delete(now_z, i).max(),
                                "worse": np.delete(worse_z, i).max()}

print(pd.DataFrame(out).T.round(2))
```

**Min-Max** collapses: the bulk maximum falls from 0.88 to 0.21, because the
range it divides by is now set entirely by the bad row, so the real data is
squeezed towards zero. **Standard** shrinks too, from 2.40 to about 1.34, since
the standard deviation is inflated by the squared distance of that one point.
**Robust** does not move at all — 1.91 before and 1.91 after — because the
median and the interquartile range cannot be shifted by a single extreme value,
which is the entire reason it exists.

That is the rule worth keeping: Min-Max is the most fragile, Standard is
affected but less so, and Robust is indifferent.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The choice is about the column, not the algorithm
Robust scaling is not uniformly better. If a column has no extreme values,
Min-Max and Standard give you a bounded or a familiar scale and nothing is
lost. Reach for Robust when you have looked at the distribution and seen a tail
— which is why @sec-histograms came first.
:::

### Task 1 — Scale, and measure the damage

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
i = gp_py["BMI"].______()           # position of the largest BMI

for name, scaler in [("minmax", MinMaxScaler()),
                     ("standard", StandardScaler()),
                     ("robust", ______())]:
    z = scaler.fit_transform(gp_py[["BMI"]]).ravel()
    bulk = np.delete(z, i)
    print(name, "outlier %.2f  bulk max %.2f" % (z[i], bulk.______()))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank returns the index of the maximum. The second is the scaler that
uses the median and IQR. The third is the largest value of the remaining rows.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
i = gp_py["BMI"].argmax()

for name, scaler in [("minmax", MinMaxScaler()),
                     ("standard", StandardScaler()),
                     ("robust", RobustScaler())]:
    z = scaler.fit_transform(gp_py[["BMI"]]).ravel()
    bulk = np.delete(z, i)
    print(name, "outlier %.2f  bulk max %.2f" % (z[i], bulk.max()))
```

The gap between the outlier and the bulk maximum is the diagnostic: 1.00
against 0.88 under Min-Max, 3.04 against 2.40 under Standard, 2.41 against 1.91
under Robust.
:::
:::

### Transformation: changing the shape, not the scale

Scaling moves a distribution and stretches it. It does not change its shape: a
skewed column scaled three ways is still skewed three ways. Changing the shape
takes a non-linear function.

Neither `pandas` nor `numpy` offers the plain moment-based skewness on its own
(`pandas` applies a sample-size correction), so define it once — the third
moment over the standard deviation cubed, exactly as the R tab does:

```{python}
def skewness(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    x = x[~np.isnan(x)]
    return np.mean((x - x.mean()) ** 3) / np.mean((x - x.mean()) ** 2) ** 1.5

print("BMI skew, as recorded:", round(skewness(gp_py["BMI"]), 2))
print("after square root    :", round(skewness(np.sqrt(gp_py["BMI"])), 2))
print("after log            :", round(skewness(np.log(gp_py["BMI"])), 2))
```

0.47 as recorded, 0.21 after the square root, −0.04 after the log. Scaling, for
contrast, leaves skewness **exactly** where it was — subtracting a constant and
dividing by a constant cannot change a shape:

```{python}
print("min-max scaled :",
      round(skewness(MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(gp_py[["BMI"]]).ravel()), 2))
print("standardised   :",
      round(skewness(StandardScaler().fit_transform(gp_py[["BMI"]]).ravel()), 2))
```

Both still 0.47.

#### Log and square root are the same idea at different strengths

It is tempting to learn these as separate recipes. They are one family. Raising
a column to a power $\lambda$ covers all of them: $\lambda = 1$ leaves the data
alone, $\lambda = 0.5$ is the square root, $\lambda = 0$ is the log, and
$\lambda = 2$ squares it. Smaller $\lambda$ pulls a long right tail in harder.

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.6
powers = {"square (2)": 2, "none (1)": 1, "sqrt (0.5)": 0.5, "log (0)": 0}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(8, 2.6))
for ax, (label, lam) in zip(axes, powers.items()):
    v = np.log(gp_py["BMI"]) if lam == 0 else gp_py["BMI"] ** lam
    z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(v.to_numpy().reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
    ax.hist(z, bins=25, color="grey")
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each panel is standardised, so only the shape differs. Read left to right and
you are turning one dial. Choosing between log and square root is choosing how
far to turn it — not choosing between two unrelated techniques.

One constraint comes with the family: the log of zero is undefined and the log
of a negative number does not exist. `BMI` is strictly positive so it is safe
here, but a column containing zeros — a count of previous admissions, say —
needs `log1p`, or a transformation built to tolerate zeros.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Feature engineering: why would $x^2$ work?

A linear model fits

$$\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

which is a straight line in $x$. If the real relationship bends, a straight
line cannot follow it. Add a squared column and you fit

$$\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2$$

which is a curve in $x$ — and still a **linear model**, because "linear" refers
to the parameters, not the features. $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ still enter as
plain multipliers, so the fitting is the same arithmetic it always was. You
changed the data, not the algorithm.

Here is the thing it buys, on a relationship that genuinely bends:

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.8
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 120)
y = 2 + 0.5 * x + 1.2 * x ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 120)

order = np.argsort(x)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.4, s=8, color="black")

for name, X in [("straight", x.reshape(-1, 1)),
                ("curved", np.column_stack([x, x ** 2]))]:
    fit = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
    pred = fit.predict(X)
    resid_sd = np.sqrt(((y - pred) ** 2).sum() / (len(y) - X.shape[1] - 1))
    print(name, "residual SD:", round(resid_sd, 2))
    ax.plot(x[order], pred[order], linewidth=1.5, label=name)

ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

A residual spread of about 3.8 for the straight line against 1.4 with the
squared term. The straight line is not wrong so much as unable. It has no
parameter capable of representing curvature, so it averages the bend away and
leaves it in the residuals.

(This is the one place where the two tabs cannot print the same numbers: the
data is simulated, and R and Python draw from different random number
generators, so the R tab's figures are close but not identical. Everything
computed from `clinic_extract.csv` matches exactly.)

#### What it costs

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

pf = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)
wide = pf.fit_transform(gp_py[scale_cols])

print("columns:", len(scale_cols), "->", wide.shape[1])
print(pf.get_feature_names_out(scale_cols))
```

Three columns became nine: each original, each square, and each pairwise
product. At degree 2 that is manageable. The growth is quadratic in the number
of features, so the same step on 30 columns gives 495, most of them nearly
duplicates of each other — and every one is a column that can be fitted on the
wrong rows.

### Task 2 — Add a term and check it earns its place

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from scipy import stats

def ols(X, y):
    """Least squares with the residual SD and p-values R reports."""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), X])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    resid = y - X @ beta
    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]
    s2 = resid @ resid / dof
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(beta / se), dof)
    return np.sqrt(s2), p

y = gp_py["systolic_BP"].values
sd1, _  = ols(gp_py[["age"]].values, y)
sd2, p2 = ols(np.column_stack([gp_py["age"], gp_py["age"] ** ______]), y)

print("residual SD, straight:", round(sd1, 3))
print("residual SD, squared :", round(______, 3))
print("p-value on the squared term:", round(p2[2], 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the power. The second is the residual SD you just computed
for the second model. `scipy` arrives with `scikit-learn`, so there is nothing
extra to install.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from scipy import stats

def ols(X, y):
    """Least squares with the residual SD and p-values R reports."""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), X])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    resid = y - X @ beta
    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]
    s2 = resid @ resid / dof
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(beta / se), dof)
    return np.sqrt(s2), p

y = gp_py["systolic_BP"].values
sd1, _  = ols(gp_py[["age"]].values, y)
sd2, p2 = ols(np.column_stack([gp_py["age"], gp_py["age"] ** 2]), y)

print("residual SD, straight:", round(sd1, 3))
print("residual SD, squared :", round(sd2, 3))
print("p-value on the squared term:", round(p2[2], 3))
```

This is the useful negative result. The residual spread moves from 10.005 to
10.003 — three thousandths of a mmHg — and the p-value on the squared term is
0.297, nowhere near significant, because this data was simulated with a
straight-line relationship between age and blood pressure. Adding $x^2$ does
not create curvature; it only lets you fit curvature that is there. Compare
with the simulated bending example above, where it was.

Note also what this does *not* do: both numbers measure fit on the same rows
the model was fitted to, so the squared version cannot score worse — an extra
parameter never increases training error. That is why the p-value is the more
informative line, and why @sec-pipeline-steps insists on a held-out split.
:::
:::

### Reflection

1. Min-Max compressed the whole `BMI` column because one value set the maximum.
   Which of the three scalers would you choose for a variable where the extreme
   values are real and clinically important, and why?
2. Standardising a column makes its mean 0 and its standard deviation 1. Does
   it make the column normally distributed? Justify your answer using the
   skewness numbers above.
3. The squared term helped on simulated curved data and not on `age`. What does
   that tell you about adding polynomial terms as a routine step?
4. Degree-2 polynomial features took 3 columns to 9. At what point does that
   stop being a feature-engineering step and start being a problem, and what
   would you look at to decide?

### Stretch

#### Stretch 1 — Find the turning power yourself
Write a loop over $\lambda$ from $-1$ to $2$ in steps of $0.25$, compute the
skewness of `BMI` raised to each power (using the log at $\lambda = 0$), and
plot skewness against $\lambda$. Read the value that brings it closest to zero
off your own plot. You have just performed a Box-Cox transformation by hand.

#### Stretch 2 — Scaling where it changes an answer
Fit a k-nearest-neighbours classifier for `diabetes` on the three numeric
columns, once unscaled and once standardised, and compare. Then explain the
difference in terms of what a Euclidean distance does when one column is
measured in hundreds and another in tens.

### What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the features are on comparable scales, that you chose the scaler
having looked at the distribution rather than by habit, that you know what the
one bad `BMI` value does to each option, and that you can add a polynomial term
and test whether it earned its place.

You cannot claim any of these numbers would survive contact with new data. Every
minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, median and IQR above was computed
from all 180 rows — including the rows you are about to hold out and call a
test set. Each one is a quantity *learned from data*, and learning it from the
wrong rows is the subject of @sec-pipeline-steps.
